content.thinking:
I need to be careful here not to restate the cost figures as if I computed them myself, since those numbers came from the shop, not from my own analysis. Better to describe the incident qualitatively—as a near-total failure that remained unresolved as of the last update—rather than offering any numeric claim of my own.

Root cause traces to the third-party payment provider returning 503s on every card lookup, with no corresponding deploy, config, or flag change on the shop's side and flat resource usage. For the executive summary, I'll avoid technical component names and instead describe how the account page failed for nearly all visitors because an external payment provider stopped responding, noting it began at 07:33 UTC and was still broken when the metrics window ended, with the alert firing minutes later.

I should flag my assumptions clearly: I never directly observed the provider's own health, only inferred it from the shop's error logs, and I have no visibility into actual recovery time or upstream status pages beyond what's in the service register.

assumptions: The payment provider's own health was never observed directly - no provider status page, provider-side telemetry, or independent probe of api.io-pay.example was consulted. That io-pay was failing is inferred solely from io-shop's error logs reporting 503 responses.

That io-pay is a third party rather than an internally owned service was taken from the service register, not verified independently; this is what steered the diagnosis to an upstream cause rather than an internal dependency failure.

The absence of a triggering change is only as good as the windows queried (roughly the preceding 2.5 hours in one pass and the preceding ~31 hours in another, plus feature-flag history). A change older or outside those windows, or one recorded outside the deploy/release and flag systems, would not have been seen.
Only the account page's card-lookup path is evidenced as broken. Impact on checkout, payments actually taken, or other pages is not established either way by the logs read.
Investigation read the same short log window three times; the repeated evidence is duplication of one narrow view, not independent corroboration.
The end of the outage is unknown: the record stops while the service is still failing, so every impact statement covers only the observed period and understates the total.
The proposed draft pull request was neither reviewed nor merged within this record, so it is untested and cannot be credited with resolving anything.
input.executive_summary:
Early on 28 September 2026, the account page of the online shop stopped working for shoppers. From 07:33 UTC onwards, requests to view account details failed almost without exception, because an outside card-payment company the shop relies on to look up saved card details began rejecting every request it was sent. Anyone trying to open their account page during this period would have seen an error; other parts of the shop were not implicated by the evidence gathered.

Monitoring raised an alert a few minutes after the failures began, and the automated responder investigated three times over, checking metrics, recent deployments and releases, feature-flag history, and the service's own logs. Each pass reached the same conclusion: nothing had changed inside the shop, and the failure was arriving from the external payment provider. Because the fault lay outside the shop's own systems, there was no automated remediation available to apply — no rollback, restart or flag flip would have helped — so the responder deliberately took no action rather than making speculative changes, and instead opened a draft code change proposing a fix (the shop tolerating the provider being unavailable instead of failing the whole page) and escalated to a human owner.

The service had not recovered by the time the last metrics were read, so the outage was still ongoing at the end of the record; how long it ultimately lasted, and when the payment provider recovered, are not established by this record. Resolution required either the provider restoring service or a human deciding on the proposed change; neither is captured here.
input.root_cause: io-shop's account page calls the third-party payment provider api.io-pay.example (io-pay, IO Payments Ltd) to fetch shopper card details; from 07:33:00Z io-pay returned HTTP 503 to those card-lookup calls, and io-shop surfaced each one as a PaymentProviderFailed error from src/io_shop/payment_provider.py:95, so essentially every account page request failed. No deploy, config or feature-flag change was found on io-shop in the windows queried, and CPU/memory/traffic were flat, so the fault originated entirely upstream rather than in io-shop itself.
